scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance was created by Loïe Fuller at the Park Theatre in Brooklyn on February 15, 1892.
It evolved from the 'skirt dance,' a burlesque form from England that reacted against academic ballet.
Fuller took the dance to Paris in 1892, performing at the Folies Bergère, where she became an icon of the Belle Époque and Art Nouveau.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a theatrical entr'acte, the dance became a symbol of technological progress and artistic abstraction.
It evokes the natural world—flowers, birds, and butterflies—through the lens of Art Nouveau.
It represented a shift toward 'total art' where movement, light, and costume are inseparable.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dancer manipulates a vast silk skirt using arms and concealed wands to create continuous, flowing shapes.
Movement is characterized by 'dance libre,' focusing on arm extensions and torso rotations rather than complex footwork.
The dancer creates curves, volutes, and arabesques, often standing in one place or moving in small circles while the fabric billows around them.
Watch for The Butterfly, The Lily, The Serpent.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (5yx3xhz_svg)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Stationary or circular path; requires a large clearance for the silk's radius.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performances were typically accompanied by orchestral or band music.
Historical records mention the use of string bands, such as the String Band of the Shropshire Light Infantry during an 1894 performance.
Listen for the Strings, Brass, Woodwinds, Percussion.
The pulse is Often 3/4 (waltz) or 4/4 (march/orchestral) at about 95 beats a minute.
The sound is typically that of a late 19th-century theater orchestra or brass band, providing a grand, rhythmic backdrop that supports the visual scale of the billowing silk.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The costume consists of hundreds of yards of lightweight China silk, sometimes arranged in a circular pattern of tapered strips.
It is often fastened at the shoulders or head rather than the waist.
Aluminum or wooden rods are sewn into the fabric to serve as arm extensions.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Loïe Fuller is the creator and primary innovator.
Notable imitators and early film performers include Annabelle Whitford Moore (Edison's 'Annabelle Serpentine Dance'), Minnie 'Renwood' Bemis, and Cinira Polónio.
While originating in the US, it became a Parisian sensation.

The Serpentine dance is a direct descendant of the English skirt dance and a precursor to modern 'dance libre.' It influenced the development of early modern dance (Isadora Duncan) and performance art.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Serpentine dance is parent of Skirt dance: The Serpentine dance is described as an evolution of the skirt dance.
Serpentine dance is influence of Modern dance: Fuller's 'dance libre' broke classical rules and influenced pioneers like Isadora Duncan.
Serpentine dance is influence of Belly dance (Isis Wings): The large pleated wings used in modern Raqs Sharqi were likely inspired by Fuller's costume.

visual_brief.costume_notes: The costume consists of hundreds of yards of lightweight China silk, sometimes arranged in a circular pattern of tapered strips. It is often fastened at the shoulders or head rather than the waist. Aluminum or wooden rods are sewn into the fabric to serve as arm extensions. The setting is a darkened stage equipped with complex multi-colored electric lighting and sometimes mirrors or glass floors for under-lighting.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Originally a theatrical entr'acte, the dance became a symbol of technological progress and artistic abstraction. It evokes the natural world—flowers, birds, and butterflies—through the lens of Art Nouveau. It represented a shift toward 'total art' where movement, light, and costume are inseparable. In its time, it also reflected the 'Fairy of Electricity' persona, celebrating the novelty of the electric age.
